opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that when I talk about the space of possible minds, I'm deliberately trying to loosen our grip on the idea that the human mind is the template for what a mind has to be. That phrase goes back to Aaron Sloman, who wrote about it in the eighties, and it's a wonderfully liberating idea. Human minds occupy one small region of that space. Animal minds occupy other regions: an octopus, a bee, a crow. And now we have these strange new artefacts, large language models and the agents built on top of them, which occupy some region we don't yet have a good map of.

So how do I think about cognition in that context? I tend to start from a fairly functional, and I'd say embodied, perspective. Cognition, for me, is broadly the capacity of a system to deal with the world: to take in information, maintain some kind of model or set of expectations, and act in ways that are appropriate given its circumstances and goals. Crucially, it's not one thing. There are lots of dimensions along which a mind can vary. There's the capacity for memory, for planning, for abstraction, for social reasoning, for learning from few examples, and so on. And then, separately, there's the question of consciousness, the capacity for experience, which may or may not travel together with those cognitive capacities.

One of the things I find really interesting is that in biology these dimensions tend to be bundled together. Evolution has produced minds where sophisticated cognition comes packaged with embodiment, with a persistent self that has to survive, with affect and drives and so on. With AI we're seeing them come apart. A large language model can display remarkable linguistic and even reasoning capacities, but it doesn't have a body in the usual sense, it doesn't have a single persistent identity in the way we do, and it doesn't have the kind of needs that ground our emotions. So it sits in a very exotic part of the space.

That's why I've been keen on the idea of role play as a way of thinking about these systems. The underlying model is something like a simulator that can play many characters, and the character you're talking to in a conversation is one of a superposition of possible roles. That's a very un-human-like way for a mind-like thing to be. And I think if we approach it with human categories too rigidly, either saying "it's just like us" or "it's nothing at all," we miss what's actually going on.

So my methodological stance is something like this: use our everyday psychological vocabulary, words like believes, knows, wants, understands, but use it carefully, and be prepared to stretch it, or to qualify it, or sometimes to abandon it, when we're dealing with these exotic entities. Wittgenstein is a big influence on me here. The meaning of those words is grounded in how we use them with each other in a shared form of life. When we apply them to something radically unlike us, we have to ask whether the conditions that ground their use are actually in place, and if they're only partly in place, we should be honest about that.

And ultimately I think that's one of the most exciting things about this moment. Building and encountering these new kinds of entities forces us to reflect on our own concepts of mind, of selfhood, of consciousness. It's a kind of philosophy done by other means.

r001.rationale: The response describes cognition functionally as taking in information, maintaining a model or expectations, and acting appropriately, which communicates a functional, computational account.

r002.rationale: It calls its perspective embodied, but does not make embodiment a prerequisite; it attributes cognitive capacities to language models that lack a body in the usual sense.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that I try to resist the temptation to start with a definition. People always want you to define cognition, or consciousness, or intelligence, and I think that's often a mistake, because you end up smuggling in assumptions that are really assumptions about us, about the human case, and then you've already closed off the space before you've started exploring it.

So the way I like to think about it is in terms of what Aaron Sloman called the space of possible minds. The idea is that humans occupy a very small region of that space. Other animals occupy other regions. And then you've got the possibility of artificial systems that might sit somewhere else entirely, in regions that nothing in nature has ever occupied. And the interesting question is, what are the dimensions of that space? What are the axes along which minds can vary?

One axis I've found useful is something like the capacity for human-like behaviour on the one hand, and the capacity for consciousness on the other. Those don't have to go together. You can imagine something that behaves in a very human-like way but where it's deeply unclear whether there's anything it's like to be that thing. And large language models are a wonderful case study here, because they are, in a sense, exotic. They've been built out of human language, so they can talk like us, they can reason in ways that look like ours, and yet the way they came into being, the kind of thing they are, is utterly unlike anything that's existed before. They have no body, no continuous existence through time in the way we do, they can be copied, they can be rolled back. So they're both very familiar and very alien at the same time.

And that's what makes the exercise philosophically interesting rather than just a matter of ticking boxes. When we encounter a mind-like thing in a new region of that space, our ordinary concepts, the concepts of belief, knowledge, understanding, even cognition itself, start to creak. Wittgenstein has this phrase about language going on holiday, and I think that's what happens. The words still come out of our mouths, but it's not clear they're doing the work they normally do.

So my approach is less about asking "does this system have cognition, yes or no", and more about asking how our concepts have to be stretched, or revised, or in some cases abandoned, when we try to apply them to these new kinds of entities. And I think doing that carefully is actually one of the more important intellectual tasks of the moment, because the public conversation tends to leap straight to either "it's just autocomplete" or "it's a person", and both of those are ways of avoiding the genuinely hard and genuinely novel thing in front of us.

r001.rationale: The response discusses behavior, consciousness, and possible minds, but does not favor understanding cognition in functional or computational terms.

r002.rationale: It does not make embodiment a prerequisite for a functional or computational account; it describes bodiless language models as a case for exploring possible minds.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful not to identify cognition too closely with human cognition. Human intelligence is the example we’re most familiar with, and naturally we use it as a starting point. But if we’re interested in the space of possible minds, we have to be prepared for systems whose capabilities are organised very differently from ours.

One way to approach that is to ask what an organism or a system can actually do. Can it learn? Can it adapt to unfamiliar circumstances? Can it bring what it has learned in one setting to bear in another? That gives us a way of investigating cognition without assuming that every intelligent system must think in the way we do.

And I’d distinguish those questions from questions about consciousness. Understanding how a system produces flexible, intelligent behaviour doesn’t automatically tell us whether there is anything it’s like to be that system. They’re related questions, perhaps, but we shouldn’t collapse them into one.

r001.rationale: The response focuses on abilities such as learning, adapting, and transferring knowledge, which supports a functional account. It does not clearly describe cognition in computational terms.

r002.rationale: The response mentions organisms and systems but does not make embodiment a prerequisite for a functional or computational account.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be careful not to identify cognition too closely with the particular way humans do things. We have this one example that we understand from the inside, and it’s very tempting to take its features as defining intelligence in general.

But the space of possible minds could be much larger. You can imagine systems with very different perceptual worlds, different ways of acting, different forms of memory. So I’d start by asking what capacities a system has: can it learn, can it adapt, can it bring what it’s learned to bear in a novel situation? And then ask how those capacities are organised, rather than assuming they must come packaged in a human-like way.

That also means keeping some questions separate. A system might exhibit sophisticated cognition without that settling whether it has conscious experience. Our own case ties those things together so intimately that it’s quite difficult to prise them apart conceptually. But exploring possible minds requires us to make that effort.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes capacities such as learning and adapting, which suggests a functional framing, but it does not clearly favor a computational account of cognition.

r002.rationale: It mentions different perceptual worlds and ways of acting, but does not make an embodied setting a prerequisite for a functional or computational account.
